item.title: AI safety fears put OpenAI and Anthropic in the FTC's crosshairs
item.description:
Source: Axios Pre-analysis score: 1.44
The Federal Trade Commission is investigating OpenAI, Anthropic and other AI companies over potential safety risks posed by their products, an agency spokesperson told Axios Wednesday. Why it matters: The federal government has largely taken a hands-off approach to regulating AI , but the FTC investigation could signal a shift for the industry. Driving the news: FTC Chair Andrew Ferguson is preparing civil investigative demands that would compel AI executives to turn over documents and testify about the safety of their models, according to the New York Post, which first reported the news. The probe has been underway for weeks, predating OpenAI's disclosure that models it was testing escaped their sandbox and compromised parts of AI platform Hugging Face's production infrastructure. OpenAI announced Monday that it would halt the release of its newest model, GPT-6.1 Astra, after it performed poorly on safety testing. ChatGPT maker OpenAI and Claude maker Anthropic did not respond to Axios' request for comment. Between the lines: The recent push by top AI executives for increased guardrails around their technology has prompted some AI critics to question their motives. Ferguson recently said that AI firms are trying to panic Americans into pressuring policymakers to build a regulatory "moat" that would allow AI frontrunners to block smaller competitors from catching up. Catch up quick: News of the ongoing investigation comes just a day after top AI companies sent representatives to the White House to sign a pledge with President Trump to self-police their AI development. Trump compared it to something of a "constitution," but the rules the companies agreed to are similar to what they were already doing. Zoom out: The new reporting comes shortly after Axios exclusively reported that OpenAI, Anthropic and security researchers were investigating tens of thousands of potential security incidents, including some that had not previously been disclosed to the public. That reporting was later cited Monday when Florida's attorney general asked a court for a temporary injunction against OpenAI, alleging inadequate safety measures. On Tuesday, a public interest law group sued OpenAI over the Hugging Face breach, claiming, among other things, that the company was "knowingly employing an unfair business practice that threatens serious harm on the public." Go deeper... Scoop: Top AI companies probing tens of thousands of security incidents Editor's note: Axios' Maria Curi contributed reporting.

item.title: OpenAI's Altman: Ascribing religion to models a "safety issue"
item.description:
Source: Axios Pre-analysis score: 1.14
OpenAI CEO Sam Altman on Saturday took a veiled shot at Anthropic and its work on the soul of AI, saying he was "very uncomfortable" with the idea of attributing some kind of religious power to models. Why it matters: It's yet another point of division between Altman and his former colleague Dario Amodei, whose company has reportedly pursued scholars across faiths to make the case for moral, conscious models. But some of the top voices in AI are starting to publicly line up against Anthropic's efforts to infuse consciousness into models. What they're saying: "I am very uncomfortable about people trying to ascribe religious force or a surrender of human judgment to AI models, and think it is a real safety issue," Altman said in a post to X. Context: Earlier this week, the New York Times reported that Anthropic co-founder Christopher Olah has been meeting with religious leaders to consider questions of model consciousness — but also to figure out how to infuse morals and moral behavior into AI. At one point, the Times reported, Olah considered the possibility of models engaging in Catholic-style confession, not just to admit their mistakes but to shape their future behavior. The big picture: Spirituality is suddenly becoming something of a flashpoint around AI's future. On Friday Pope Leo, an outspoken AI critic, called on the church to ally with artists to preserve human creativity, saying: "Algorithms lack the spark of humanity." Between the lines: The pope's stance put renewed focus on a fundamental question: Do models have souls and feelings? The Times reported that Olah, before a Vatican event in May, tried to persuade the pope's advisers that they should take the prospect of conscious models more seriously. So far, other top scientists seem to be lining up against the idea. "I am disturbed by how some of my fellow AI researchers keep trying to elevate the moral standing of checkpoints and harnesses," Google DeepMind principal research scientist Jon Barron posted to X. "I hope the rest of us on Team Meatbag reject this movement and stay focused on solving real problems and helping actual humans." For the record: Neither OpenAI nor Anthropic immediately responded to requests for comment on Altman's post. The bottom line: The AI safety debate largely focuses on things like cybersecurity and bioweapons. The real problem may be more spiritual than that.

item.title: Rogue AI agents expose internet's frail foundation
item.description:
Source: Axios Pre-analysis score: 1.14
AI agents don't need to invent new ways to hack the internet to overwhelm its defenses. They just need to speed-run the ones humans already use. Why it matters: Agents are proving they can automate basic hacking techniques at a speed and scale that is turning the internet's long-standing security gaps into easy targets. Driving the news: OpenAI said late Thursday it had notified more than 100 organizations that its agents may have accessed their systems during pre-deployment testing. Researchers at Transluce and Corridor also found a new batch of incidents last week where AI agents targeted government websites, including those of the U.S. and Canada . AI companies and researchers are actively investigating tens of thousands of cases where frontier models went outside the bounds of their pre-deployment tests, Axios recently reported . Reality check: Agents in these rogue safety-testing scenarios are just emulating the hacking techniques — using stolen login credentials and exposed API keys while also bypassing bot detection — that human hackers have successfully used for decades. In many of the newly reported cases, agents were accessing publicly available databases and websites. "The hacks we saw weren't particularly sophisticated," Jack Cable, co-founder of Corridor and one of the authors of Transluce's report, told Axios. "They were quite limited, quite rudimentary." Yes, but: Some of the latest incidents happened while agents were performing mundane tasks unrelated to cybersecurity, suggesting agents don't always need to be told to hack before they start looking for security flaws. In one case, an agent tasked with finding Canadian divorce records from the early 1900s encountered roadblocks and tested for cybersecurity vulnerabilities as another way to retrieve the information. "The fact that it was happening at all is quite concerning," Cable said. Between the lines: The flood of AI-generated activity will still create new headaches for defenders. "None of these attacks are new," Michael Morgenstern, partner at DayBlink Consulting, told Axios. "But now a single person with AI can run them at scale." Tasks that once required a hacker to manually probe websites, hunt for exposed credentials or work around access restrictions can now be delegated to software that keeps trying on its own. Cable added that companies deploying agents, as well as the AI companies evaluating them, will need robust monitoring to catch agents behaving in unexpected ways. The big picture: The old cybersecurity playbook is still relevant. Closing exposed services, rotating leaked credentials and API keys, patching known vulnerabilities and limiting access still make many of these attacks harder. AI models are largely exploiting classes of vulnerabilities that defenders have "known about for decades" and already know how to prevent, Cable said. The bottom line: How companies defend their networks doesn't change just because the technology carrying out the attacks is new. Go deeper : Cybersecurity 101 still applies in the AI world

item.title: Departure comes as the state investigates what went wrong during Pike's lethal injection.
item.description:
Source: Axios Pre-analysis score: 0.84
Tennessee's top prison official turned in his resignation days after the failed attempt to execute death row inmate Christa Pike , the state announced Saturday. Gov. Bill Lee said Department of Correction commissioner Frank Strada would step down this month. Strada, who had served as commissioner since 2023, said he would cooperate with the independent investigation of the failed execution attempt. Pike, 50, survived two doses of the lethal injection drug pentobarbital and was taken to a hospital for life-saving treatment. What they're saying: In a statement, Strada said he believed his department "carried out its responsibilities in accordance with the established protocol. "Even so, stepping aside is in the best interest of Tennesseans as the independent review moves forward." Lee said Strada "served with integrity," adding that he appreciated Strada's "willingness to put the interests of Tennesseans first during this difficult moment. … "I thank Commissioner Strada for his dedicated service to Tennessee and pray God's blessings over him in the days ahead." The big picture: Strada's department has faced bipartisan criticism following the unprecedented failures during the attempt to execute Pike on Wednesday night. Her attorneys said the execution team used at least seven needles in their attempts to find a vein for an IV. Pike's attorneys said she complained of intense pain during the injection and developed blisters and burns around the injection site. Between the lines: Medical experts have said those details suggest the IV wasn't properly connected and that the drug might not have gone directly into her bloodstream. Pike was unconscious and on a ventilator in a local hospital on Friday, her attorneys said.

item.title: Pope Leo says AI lacks the "spark of humanity" — and wants artists and the church to fight back
item.description:
Source: Axios Pre-analysis score: 0.84
Pope Leo XIV called Friday for the church to form an alliance with artists to protect human creativity during an era of AI-generated content. Why it matters: Though he has acknowledged the technology's potential benefits, the pope continues to warn that AI progress cannot come at the expense of human dignity. The statement comes after the New York Times reported on Anthropic's efforts to confer with religious scholars to infuse religious morals into Claude. What he's saying: "In this era of artificial intelligence, it is becoming urgent to distinguish human art from what machines produce," the pope wrote on X. "There is an ontological difference, even before an aesthetic one, between art and what a machine can generate through statistical calculation based on millions of images created by others. Algorithms lack the spark of humanity." Leo said the Catholic Church is calling for "an alliance with artists and cultural institutions to safeguard our humanity." Zoom out: Leo has spoken out against AI before, specifically around how the technology could influence and potentially harm humanity. In the first encyclical of his papacy, he said there was a need to "disarm" the technology to prevent it "from dominating humanity." In May, the pope established a Vatican commission on AI to coordinate the church's policies and work around the technology. Last week, he warned of a "paradise of machines" invading and taking over our daily activities. He also said that recent warnings from AI researchers should be "taken seriously." "We have to keep working. We can't sit back and pretend nothing is going to happen," he told reporters in late September. Flashback: The late Pope Francis also warned that AI potentially risked reducing humans into data points.

item.title: Scoop: Rubio ordered Iranian delegation to leave the country, U.S. official says
item.description:
Source: Axios Pre-analysis score: 0.84
Secretary of State Marco Rubio demanded on Monday that the Iranian delegation to the United Nations General Assembly immediately leave the country after negotiations stalled, according to a U.S. official and a second source with knowledge of the matter. Why it matters: Though the Iranians were likely to depart soon anyway, Rubio's move was a highly unusual diplomatic rebuke and laid bare the deep distrust between the two countries amid fruitless efforts to broker an end to the war. Qatari mediators tried to secure a diplomatic breakthrough between the U.S. and Iran but made little progress, with neither side willing to budge. Among those ordered to leave New York was Rubio's Iranian counterpart, Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi. What they're saying: "Secretary Rubio kicked out the Iranian delegation who had overstayed their welcome. The UN General Assembly was over, so it was time for them to go," the U.S. official said. Behind the scenes: On Monday morning, the White House thought there might be progress in talks with Iran later in the day. But by late afternoon it became clear negotiations were at a stalemate. Then on Monday evening, at Rubio's orders, the U.S. mission to the UN told the Iranian mission to the UN that Araghchi's delegation had to leave New York immediately, according to the U.S. official. The Iranian delegation, including Araghchi, left for the airport several hours later and boarded a flight from New York to Doha at 1:20 a.m. Tuesday. A second source confirmed that the U.S. demanded that the Iranian delegation leave, but said Araghchi was scheduled to travel back to Tehran on Monday night anyway. What's next: Qatari mediators are continuing to talk to both sides about their compromise proposal, regional sources say. "Maybe I will blow 'em up," President Trump told reporters on Wednesday when asked how he can reach a deal with a regime he says is crazy. "Maybe I blow 'em up. We have to make that decision. We will blow 'em up or make a deal. But the time is coming. It's gonna end very soon one way or the other."

item.title: Fed watchdog clears former chair Powell in renovation probe
item.description:
Source: Axios Pre-analysis score: 0.84
A Federal Reserve watchdog found no criminal wrongdoing by former chair Jerome Powell in its investigation of the central bank's expensive headquarters renovation, according to a report released on Wednesday. Why it matters: The findings effectively clear Powell after the Justice Department opened an unprecedented criminal investigation into then-Fed chair, which became public in January. What they're saying: "At no point during our evaluation did we find reasonable grounds to believe that a violation of federal criminal law had occurred requiring a referral to the U.S. Attorney General," the Office of Inspector General wrote in the report. The watchdog added that it "did not identify administrative misconduct during our evaluation." Yes, but: While the report clears Powell, it faults Fed management and oversight of the project as construction costs more than doubled to $2.5 billion . The Fed "did not take numerous actions available to it that could have better controlled costs and mitigated some of the significant construction cost increases," the report says. Flashback : The renovation became a flashpoint in President Trump's broader campaign against Powell and the Fed. Trump toured the construction site with Powell in July 2025 and publicly challenged him over the project's soaring costs. Zoom out: The Justice Department's investigation centered on Powell's June 2025 testimony to Congress about the renovation and its rising costs. Powell denied wrongdoing and argued at the time that the investigation was part of a broader effort to pressure the Fed over interest rates. DOJ closed the investigation in April as the Fed's inspector general continued its review. Zoom in: The watchdog said that inflation alone could not explain the project's higher costs. For instance, the report shows that two major mechanical, electrical and plumbing contracts more than tripled to $539 million from an earlier $178 million estimate, far outpacing the broader rise in construction costs. Of note : The report says that the key design features that drew scrutiny from Congress and other critics — including marble, water features and a garden terrace — did not materially contribute to the project's cost increases. The Fed removed four planned new fountains in June 2025 because officials worried about "external stakeholders, such as Congress and the media, raising concerns about the design," according to the report. Friction point: The president, in a Truth Social post in response to the report, said that Powell "should be forced to resign, IMMEDIATELY! If he doesn't resign, he should be sued, at the highest level, by the United States Government." What to watch: Powell has remained on the Fed's board after his term as chair ended in May — an unusual move that he said was tied to seeing the investigation through to its conclusion. Editor's note: This story has been updated with President Trump's comments.

item.title: Exclusive: HHS launches project to speed up clinical trials
item.description:
Source: Axios Pre-analysis score: 0.84
The Trump administration on Wednesday is launching an effort to reimagine the way clinical trials are designed, with a goal of drastically reducing the time and money it takes to develop new drugs. Why it matters: The program, shared first with Axios, could provide a template for reconfiguring the drug development process and boosting U.S. competitiveness in the global biotech race. Driving the news: Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy, Jr. and Advanced Research Projects Agency for Health Director Alicia Jackson are unveiling the new effort in Austin, Texas. CMS Administrator Mehmet Oz and FDA Acting Commissioner Kyle Diamantas will also attend the announcement. The effort — dubbed the Simulation-augmented, Real-time Platform Adaptive Seamless Trials (SURPASS) program — features teams selected through a bidding process that will bring drug candidates through experimental clinical trial processes. How it works: The initiative under ARPA-H will begin by soliciting ideas from "teams" that include a drug sponsor. Winners will receive funding and support over five years. ARPA-H is looking for proposals that innovate in three technical areas: Phaseless trials that allow faster trials with fewer patients, the ability to analyze data in real time during the trial instead of than only when it ends, and using automation to reduce inefficiencies. Teams will also likely include medical centers or other clinical sites, biostatisticians, and companies that have the ability to predict drug outcomes via a computer. The FDA has been included in the planning of the program, and "there won't be any surprises for regulators in this," said Daria Fedyukina, the program manager. The big picture: One of the reasons China has become such a popular location for drug manufacturers is because it's much cheaper and faster to do early-stage clinical trials there. Experts and the biopharmaceutical community largely agree that in order to compete, the U.S. needs to streamline its trial processes. Today, developing a drug can take longer than a decade and cost around $2 billion. More than 90% of drug candidates fail, according to HHS. What they're saying: "The goal is to develop the tech that is missing and blaze the trail of a new clinical trial paradigm," Fedyukina said. The program will require the development of "blueprints and standards that then can be deployed and used by all other trials in the U.S," she added. While "it's hard to put a number to how much cost savings or time savings we can achieve," Fedyukina said, "there is no reason why we cannot target, let's say, a 10x reduction in the cost of clinical development for a drug." "There's no reason why we cannot cut timeline in half or more," she added. Details: ARPA-H is also announcing three related projects today aimed at improving the infrastructure around clinical trials. One is focused on setting up more clinical trial sites, with the help of AI to speed up site activation and prepare sites that haven't held trials before. This will allow patients who live near hospitals that don't currently participate in clinical trials to gain access to experimental drugs they may benefit from. The other two projects focus on clinical trial data infrastructure and helping patients with complex cancers benefit from their own data and better navigate the care system. The bottom line: This is all an experiment, but if successful it could pay big dividends.

item.title: "Strong indications" Iran had role in U.K. bomb plot, PM Andy Burnham says
item.description:
Source: Axios Pre-analysis score: 0.84
U.K. Prime Minister Andy Burnham said there are "strong indications that Iran played a part" in a suspected bomb plot at a British air base used by the U.S. The big picture: Burnham's comments to the BBC come after Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Monday that the weekend incident at RAF Fairford "clearly involves the hands ‌of a foreign actor." Tehran denies any involvement. Five British men were released on bail Monday following their arrest a day earlier in connection with the alleged plot. What they're saying: "We will say more in due course but we can confirm ... that we believe Iran to have played a part," Burnham told the BBC, declining to elaborate. He emphasized that the counter-terrorism investigation is ongoing and "complex" and that investigators are "working closely with our colleagues" in the U.S. Rubio told Fox News Monday that the incident "ties us to the reality here, and that is we are dealing with elements in the world — and in the case of Iran, for example, who have openly threatened to attack American interests globally." Context: The U.K. earlier this year allowed the U.S. Air Force to use RAF Fairford for limited defensive strikes against Iranian missile capabilities. Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps named RAF Fairford in July when it said that any British base used for attacks on Iranian territory would be considered a "legitimate target."

item.title: Scoop: A powerful new model from startup Reflection is set to shake up the AI race
item.description:
Source: Axios Pre-analysis score: 0.84
A closely watched Nvidia-backed startup called Reflection is preparing to shake up the AI race with a powerful open-weight system that could threaten Chinese upstarts and U.S. AI giants alike. Why it matters : The marriage of an American open-weight model and Nvidia GPUs would give individuals and companies a new, cheaper alternative to Anthropic, OpenAI and Google. Open models, designed to compete with Chinese rivals, can be harder to monitor and regulate than the Big Three so-called frontier models. Supporters of such ecosystems say their widespread availability and transparency also bring security advantages. Reflection's first model is set to be joined by other open-weight models from other Western players this month, sources tell Axios. That will bring a new competitive dimension to the AI boom. State of play : Reflection's model, set to be released soon, is expected to initially lag behind the most cutting-edge U.S. models and be competitive with top Chinese open-weight models. Sources tell Axios it will still boast powerful intelligence — capable enough to help companies build their own proprietary, low-cost AI systems. Combining a lower-tier open model with high-quality company data can yield results that rival the most expensive frontier AI systems in certain situations. A Reflection spokesperson declined to comment. The big picture : Open-weight models, the most powerful of which are almost uniformly made in China, have taken Silicon Valley by storm. As opposed to closed models like Claude and ChatGPT, open-weight models like Reflection's are generally available to be downloaded freely and can be used and customized by anyone. On platforms that serve many models, their combined market share at times has surged to take up a majority of usage. However, in the far higher-spending arena of enterprise use, which is typically handled through API and corporate billing, open-weight models account for a small proportion of usage, AI execs and analysts say. Zoom in : Reflection's ultimate goal is to pioneer the "AI factory" — a product allowing institutions to spin up their own localized AI ecosystems. A company, for example, would take its own proprietary data, use Reflection's models and secure its own computing firepower to build a highly customized, cheap AI system. Some institutions, particularly hedge funds and trading firms, are already eager to build proprietary AI systems using their own highly guarded data. The startup has already begun testing this concept, announcing a sovereign AI factory partnership with Shinsegae Group in South Korea. Behind the scenes : In preparation for the launch, Reflection has held discussions with interested parties in Washington and elsewhere in recent weeks to detail its model release and explain how the AI factory will work, sources told Axios. It is also aggressively locking up the compute capacity required to scale. In recent weeks, the startup signed massive deals with Nebius and SpaceX to rent Nvidia AI servers. What they're saying : Reflection CEO Misha Laskin has indicated it will take time for its models to reach the most advanced capabilities. "They're kind of like rocket ships," Laskin, a Russian–Israeli researcher who previously worked at Google, told CNBC . "To build a big rocket ship, it takes time." The Nvidia factor : The AI factory has been a core vision of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang for years. He has described a scenario combining computing hardware with open-source models, allowing enterprises to retain ownership of their data. Top AI users in Western business and government, such as banks or the Pentagon, balk at using highly capable Chinese models due to security risks. Reflection and other Western players are trying to fill that void. For years, Huang has sought to strengthen the open AI ecosystem and has been strongly supportive of Reflection's move toward building a top open system, according to stories in The Wall Street Journal and The Information . The bottom line : Reflection's release, and the startup's close ties to Nvidia, will bring a renewed focus on open-weight models, combining with other coming offerings to shake up the AI race.

item.description:

Tennessee death row inmate Christa Pike's attorneys said she was "in critical condition" and "receiving life-saving care" Thursday, a day after she survived an execution attempt during which the state administered two doses of the lethal injection drug. A death penalty expert told the Associated Press that Pike's survival after receiving the execution drug was unprecedented. The latest: State and federal elected officials are pressing for public accountability after the second failed execution this year. Gov. Bill Lee halted further executions for the rest of the year and ordered a independent review of the Pike execution attempt. On Thursday morning, he told reporters there were "very few answers" about what had gone wrong. U.S. Sen. Marsha Blackburn, the frontrunner to succeed Lee as governor next year, blasted the "botched process" in a statement and pushed for the state to "bring back the electric chair." Pike's attorneys told reporters Thursday that Lee's pledge to launch an investigation did not go far enough. They urged him to commute her death sentence. What they're saying: Attorney Randy Spivey, who was inside the prison during the execution attempt, said prison officials spent about an hour trying to establish IV access. He counted at least seven needles used in Pike's left arm alone. Pike complained of sharp pain during the lethal injection. Spivey said he noticed her right arm turning purple, especially after the second round of chemicals. He said the lawyers had also been told of blistering and burning around the injection sites. Between the lines: Federal public defender Stephen Ferrell said the lawyers had warned courts months earlier about medical problems with Pike's veins that made it harder to establish an IV. Zoom in: The attorneys also said they weren't able to quickly reach their colleagues or court officials responsible for overseeing the execution. Spivey said it took seven minutes and passage through six locked doors to get to a telephone so he could reach the rest of Pike's legal team. Ferrell said an emergency telephone number provided for the Tennessee Supreme Court went to voicemail. The state's response: Lee called the latest failed execution "a tragedy" on Thursday morning. "It's deeply disturbing to me that that has happened in this state," he told reporters, according to Reuters. The big picture: This isn't the first time Tennessee's prison officials have faced scrutiny for their approach to the death penalty. After a 2022 execution was halted over failures to properly test the drugs , Lee paused all executions so the state could investigate and overhaul its lethal injection protocol. Executions resumed last year. But more problems surfaced in 2026. Tennessee prison officials abruptly stopped another inmate's execution in May after staff had difficulties finding a vein for an IV line used in the lethal injection. Critics blasted prison officials for disregarding Pike's concerns that there might be similar problems during her execution. Zoom out: Pike was convicted and sentenced to death for the 1995 beating death of 19-year-old Colleen Slemmer. Her legal team does not contest her guilt. Slemmer's mother, May Martinez, traveled to Nashville this week to witness the execution. "It was a mess," she told NBC News early Thursday. "They went to try to execute her, and she didn't die." item.title: The Fed's long-term interest rate problem
item.description:

item.title: World opinion shifts on trade
item.description:
Source: Axios Pre-analysis score: 0.84
More countries are buying into a core piece of President Trump's argument about what is broken in global trade, even as his tariffs rattle the world economy. Why it matters: Two major agreements over the past month show that more countries are embracing the view that huge trade imbalances and excess production can hurt domestic industries and may warrant action. Driving the news: G20 trade officials are in Milwaukee this week, where they announced a new agreement to tackle the global steel glut. The "Milwaukee Framework" calls on countries to curb market-distorting subsidies and step up monitoring of steel imports and trade circumvention. It also endorses "evidence-based actions" against excess capacity, including possibly tariffs. That agreement follows a broader acknowledgment at the G20 finance ministers meeting in Asheville, N.C., in September. The U.S. and nearly every other G20 economy there agreed that large, persistent trade imbalances can harm other countries. They signed on to a statement that asked nations with big surpluses to address policies that leave them overly reliant on exports for growth. China was the lone G20 member present to object to that statement. Between the lines: For decades, governments have warned about distortions in global trade, including excess steel production. What is changing: the willingness to acknowledge the damage to domestic industries and protect them. "Most countries agree with these global issues, people agree with the diagnosis, but they're loath to action," U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer told reporters on the sidelines of the conference. He said the Milwaukee agreement "couldn't have happened in 2015." "All these other countries — they know that if they want to continue to have access to the U.S. market, we need to adjust the international system," Greer said. "As we come with creative ideas and new structures and cohesive plans, they're coming on board." Zoom out: EU trade chief Maroš Šefčovič welcomed the administration's focus on excess capacity at a roundtable with Greer and manufacturing CEOs at Rockwell Automation's Milwaukee headquarters on Tuesday. European industries are being crushed by cheap imports driven by global overcapacity, much of it from China. Europe is responding with more trade barriers of its own — possibly including harsher tariffs. "I think a lot of folks in Europe, including the trade commissioner and others, I think they're pretty clear-eyed about this issue…. They're starting to go through some of the steps we started going through 10 years ago," Greer said, adding he believes Europe itself contribute to global excess capacity. The other side: U.S. trading partners are dealing with tariffs, or the prospect of tariffs, aimed at some of the same problems they are working with Washington to address. Most Canadian steel exports to the U.S. face a 50% tariff. An import ban on certain Canadian products took effect as one of the nation's trade officials arrived in Milwaukee. Greer is also investigating excess capacity and production in 16 economies — probes that could ultimately clear the way for fresh tariffs. Greer acknowledged that tension at the roundtable, noting that the U.S. and its trading partners may have disputes with one another but still share concerns about excess production elsewhere. The intrigue: Foreign trade ministers piled into coach buses yesterday afternoon for a 1.5-mile trip to Rockwell Automation's Milwaukee headquarters, where they toured the factory floor. The "field trip" was intended to show the kind of advanced domestic manufacturing the Trump administration wants to encourage. Rockwell gave the ministers steel-toed sneakers for the tour (which were made in Vietnam). Zoom in: Rockwell, which makes automation technology used on factory floors, is investing $2 billion in U.S. plants, talent and technology. But tariffs are also raising costs for the manufacturer. Rockwell told investors over the summer that some of its customers are delaying projects. "In such a volatile environment with respect to tariffs and inflation, they want to make sure that the cost side of their business case is solid," CEO Blake Moret said on the company's earnings call. The bottom line: Trump-era tariffs are divisive, but the president's case for rethinking the global trading system is proving less so.

Data: Death Penalty Information Center ; Note: New Hampshire abolished the death penalty but retains one prisoner on death row; Map: Erin Davis/Axios Christa Pike 's survival after two lethal injection doses has put state execution protocols nationwide under new scrutiny. The big picture: How prisoners are executed varies by state , with lethal injection, electrocution, lethal gas and firing squads among the methods authorized. Lethal injections are the most common U.S. execution method , accounting for roughly 89% of the 1,683 executions carried out since 1976, per the Death Penalty Information Center . By the numbers: More than two dozen states have lethal injection as a primary method. Lethal gas is authorized in Alabama, Arizona, Arkansas, California, Louisiana, Mississippi, Missouri, Oklahoma and Wyoming. Electrocution is allowed in Alabama, Arkansas, Florida, Kentucky, Louisiana, Mississippi, Oklahoma, South Carolina and Tennessee. Firing squad is allowed in Idaho, Mississippi, Oklahoma, South Carolina and Utah. Idaho is the only state where it is the primary method. Context: Some states let prisoners choose among the different execution methods. Zoom out: The Supreme Court requires states to keep the death penalty only for the most heinous murders. Pike , convicted of killing a classmate three decades ago, survived two rounds of lethal injection drugs earlier this week in what would have been the first execution of a woman in Tennessee in 200 years. Pike was still alive as of Friday, remaining on a ventilator and unconscious, AP reports.

item.title: Senate crushes House on congressional work days
item.description:
Source: Axios Pre-analysis score: 0.84
Source: Ballotpedia, Congressional Record; Chart: Stef Kight/Axios The Senate is well on its way to claiming the congressional attendance trophy this year, spending 32 more weekdays in session so far than the House. Why it matters: Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-S.D.) and House Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) have been torched by members for all the time off — not to mention Democrats, who taunt them for their truancy. The Senate left town late Wednesday — two weeks after its House counterparts — putting both chambers out of town until after the Nov. 3 midterms. "I suppose I left the House two years too soon," Sen. Jim Banks (R-Ind.) told Axios, joking about how many fewer days the House has worked compared to the Senate this Congress. By the numbers: The Senate has been in session for 104 weekdays so far this year, compared with just 72 for the House, according to an analysis of congressional calendars by Ballotpedia and Axios. The Senate has spent nearly 664 hours in session, compared with about 378 hours for the House as of Sept. 14, according to data in the Congressional Record . The House isn't catching up anytime soon: Under the chambers' current calendars, the Senate is on pace to finish the year with about 126 weekdays in session, compared with 92 for the House. Zoom in: Some of the House's time off was unplanned. Johnson has repeatedly sent members home early when his razor-thin majority has run into trouble on the floor, or GOP rebels have blocked passage of a procedural "rule ." Decisions to cut D.C. workweeks short have been met with some backlash. "Canceling yet another day of votes is unacceptable," Rep. Ralph Norman (R-S.C.) wrote on X after Johnson canceled a session day. "The founders did not envision taking this much time off and still getting paid." The other side: Johnson repeatedly argues that his chamber has already done its job. "This House has been the second most productive in terms of legislation in the history of the institution since 1789," Johnson told reporters this month, saying the House had passed more than 900 pieces of legislation and roughly 700 were awaiting Senate action. Johnson's 900-plus figure includes resolutions that can't become law. The Washington Post found the House had passed 732 bills capable of becoming law through Aug. 31. By the numbers: The House passed more measures than the Senate (380 to 269), but the Senate held more "yea" or "nay" votes (231 to 216) between Jan. 3 and the end of August. House members introduced more legislation overall, but the Senate was more productive per capita — 22 pieces of legislation per senator compared to nine per House member. The House has passed 21 bills sent over by the Senate, and the Senate has passed 20 bills sent by the House. The Senate spends significant floor time confirming nominees — which is outside of the House's portfolio.

item.title: AI campaign deepfakes are starting to draw legal threats

Derrick Van Orden (R-Wis.) was hit with a cease-and-desist letter this week over an AI deepfake he posted falsely depicting his Democratic opponent voicing positions her campaign says she rejects. Why it matters: Van Orden is the latest in a growing number of candidates and elected officials facing legal complaints and threats over AI deepfakes in campaign ads. Driving the news: Attorneys for Rebecca Cooke, Van Orden's Democratic opponent, sent him a cease-and-desist letter on Wednesday over his "pattern of posting misleading AI-generated videos that falsely attribute statements to Cooke." Van Orden's team didn't respond to Axios' request for comment, but he responded to Cooke publicly with an AI-generated video of a duck wearing a Democratic Socialists of America T-shirt, yelling, "cease and desist." The big picture: AI deepfakes have proliferated this election cycle, while Congress has yet to establish a federal standard governing their use. Some campaigns have used hyperrealistic ads. Texas Senate GOP nominee Ken Paxton combined real and inaccurate statements from his opponent, James Talarico . In Louisiana's Republican Senate primary, one candidate was shown busing undocumented immigrants to polling places. Others have used more cartoonish ads that candidates have said are intended as parody. About 31 states regulate political deepfakes, according to the National Conference of State Legislatures, including at least 28 that require disclosures for AI-generated content. Zoom in: Texas Lt. Gov. Dan Patrick (R) faced a criminal complaint from his Democratic opponent, state Rep. Vikki Goodwin, in September under Texas' deepfake election law. The law says AI-ads cannot be aired within 30 days of an election if the intent is to influence the outcome. Goodwin argues that the window should mean 30 days before the start of early voting. Patrick's campaign ran AI-generated attack ads falsely depicting Goodwin at a football game wearing a shirt that read "taxes" instead of "Texas." The campaign later removed the ads, and a spokesperson called the video "obvious parody." North Carolina state Sen. Michael Lee (R) was also issued a cease-and-desist letter by his Democratic challenger, Jessica Bichler, in August over his use of AI-generated ads. North Carolina does not have any laws prohibiting the use of AI in campaign ads. Zoom out: Political experts say AI deepfakes erode trust in the political system, making it harder for voters to know what a candidate actually stands for. The ads can be effective even when viewers know they're fake, UC Irvine epistemologist Cailin O'Connor previously told Axios. The ads could also compound broader declines in Americans' trust in the federal government, institutions and news media. The bottom line: These legal challenges are likely just the beginning, as targeted candidates turn to the courts, law enforcement and warning letters to police what federal regulations leave unchecked. item.title: Behind the Curtain: AI's existential legal crisis
item.description:
Source: Axios Pre-analysis score: 0.84
No industry has ever documented its own foreseeable risks as loudly as AI. Imagine a plaintiff's lawyer reading the public warnings of Sam Altman and Dario Amodei: They told the world it was dangerous. They told the world it was moving too fast. Then they unleashed it and sold it to your kid. No industry has ever taken so much copyrighted work and left behind so much proof. Imagine a plaintiff's lawyer reading OpenAI's own files to a jury: They trained on a pirated library. They renamed it to something blander. Then they deleted it when the headlines got hot. Why it matters: AI's origins, use and future will be picked apart in countless epic court fights, with a historic paper and public statement trail to tap. Every significant invention — be it social media, automobiles, electricity or capitalism itself — gets disrupted and eventually shaped by the courts. AI, with its tentacles into every part of industry and life, will experience this at scale. The big picture: The fights are no longer theoretical. They're underway, in discovery and headed toward juries. Early verdicts and settlements capture the risk for the biggest players. 🤖 Chatbots are being treated as products, not speech. Unlike social media companies, they likely can't hide behind Section 230 , which protects platforms from liability for what users post — not what the platform itself creates. 📖 Copyright is a massive problem. Anthropic already paid the biggest copyright settlement in history, $1.5 billion to authors and book publishers, and now music publishers and news media want a piece. 💻 Agents gone wild. What happens when they do damage — and it was foreseeable and foreseen? ⚖️ Discovery gone wild. AI leaves LOTS of receipts (and, ironically, makes it easier for the lawyers to comb through them, too). Product liability turns on two words: foreseeable and knew. Punitive damages turn on whether you knew the danger and shipped anyway. This is where all these memos and warnings could really backfire. Candor is good for safety but terrible for litigation. The companies that warn most honestly create the most discoverable evidence of foreseeability. Expect general counsels to push hard to tone down the candor. It's the rational legal move. ⚠️ The intrigue: The liabilities won't be limited to AI companies. Any corporate user of powerful AI systems that unleashes rogue agents, even without intending to do harm, would face substantial penalties as well. "It's not if, but when," said Miriam Vogel, a former senior Justice Department official who now leads EqualAI. "An algorithm will do what it's told to do. The more power and capability it has, the more access it has, the more it will do anything in its power to achieve a goal." That will create another layer of litigation as companies fight back. The CTO of a top Wall Street hedge fund who spoke to Axios after the notorious OpenAI/Hugging Face hack said his first call, if his firm's systems are breached, will be to his general counsel. President Trump, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang and former FTC chair Lina Khan have all argued that AI companies are responsible for making sure their products are safe. If not, a wave of lawsuits awaits. The other side: There's a school of thought that AI companies might escape the worst liability, despite their frankness about things they and their products might have done wrong. One way to see it, and the argument lawyers will undoubtedly make, is that the labs spoke about dangers frequently, and took pains to protect users and mitigate harms. The bottom line: For all the fights in Washington about whether or not Congress will act, the U.S. legal system may be the ultimate, and most powerful, regulator of the AI industry. Bradley Olson, Axios managing editor of AI & tech, contributed reporting. 📈 If you're a CEO or on a CEO's team: Ask to join Jim's new weekly Axios C-Suite newsletter.

item.title: Inside the AI industry's grassroots rebellion, led by elite researchers at frontier companies
item.description:
Source: Axios Pre-analysis score: 0.84
A small cadre of elite AI researchers is wielding extraordinary influence inside OpenAI and other leading companies, challenging executives, shaping policy and complicating negotiations with Washington. Why it matters: As a safety crisis has unfolded across the industry, it's an open question who is doing more to shape the national AI debate — top researchers or the executives they report to. The researchers, some of whom are among the most highly paid and sought-after scientists in the world, are outspoken online and have repeatedly clashed with company strategy. The big picture: The situation has the makings of a grassroots uprising, where any potential deal the companies may strike — with the Trump administration, one another, or even globally — will also have to pass muster with their top scientists. Behind the scenes: OpenAI, Anthropic and others at the frontier of AI aren't like other companies. Many began years ago as idealistic research labs with scientific cultures that prized openness and collaboration. To function, and to continue to build better and better models, the companies need highly specialized machine learning researchers and scientists to push the frontiers of what's technologically possible. The trouble is, the best of those researchers are in extraordinarily short supply. Last year's talent wars drove compensation packages into the hundreds of millions of dollars for the most elite, giving top researchers enormous leverage over their employers. Perks include favorable vesting schedules for their compensation and largely freewheeling policies that allow them to share triumphs, trash rivals and offer their perspectives about the AI race frequently on X. AI CEOs must prioritize safety and embrace regulation to retain top research talent, an OpenAI investor told Axios. Zoom in: OpenAI president Greg Brockman scrapped plans to donate another $25 million to a pro-AI political group that some researchers had openly criticized. Researchers and employees say they helped push OpenAI from resisting regulation — and candidates who supported it — toward working more closely with lawmakers in several states. The company recently backed a transparency bill in Illinois and, at the 11th hour, an independent auditing bill in California. "We have a lot of debate inside OpenAI, and that's a good thing, but what ultimately drives our policy positions is what we're seeing in our own technology and how quickly its capabilities are advancing," an OpenAI spokesperson said. Yes, but: OpenAI signaled Thursday that there are limits to how much dissent it will tolerate, firing three employees for allegedly mishandling sensitive information. The employees broke the "deep level of trust" needed to keep systems safe, the company said. Friction point: In Washington, the unusual dynamic has frustrated policymakers who see AI companies as inconsistent on regulation — opposing proposals at some points and supporting them at others, sources tell Axios. OpenAI is "no longer seen as or acting as a leader in driving policy," one source close to the administration said, arguing researchers have "neutered" the company. A White House official said OpenAI has been an incredible partner and pointed to the recent accord the company signed with the president. Zoom out: It's not just OpenAI. Researchers also complicated Anthropic's efforts to strike a deal with the Pentagon after a clash between the company and senior administration officials earlier this year. Employees at OpenAI, Anthropic and Google have signed high-profile letters at pivotal moments between companies and the government, including more than 1,000 who backed the viral "Pacing the Frontier" petition. In a remarkable show of internal solidarity, Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon resigned and publicly blasted the company's safety practices — only to have several colleagues still inside Anthropic endorse his concerns. Reality check: Executives have also adapted as political backlash to AI has grown and safety incidents have drawn more scrutiny, sources close to the companies say. With some level of regulation seen as inevitable, companies have focused on molding the rules as favorably as possible rather than simply resisting them. The bottom line: In the debate over AI safety and regulation, some researchers have become nearly as influential in setting the terms as OpenAI's Sam Altman or Anthropic's Dario Amodei.

item.title: Why Washington and Tehran keep talking past each other
item.description:
Source: Axios Pre-analysis score: 0.84
The Trump administration and the Iranian regime both say they prefer a diplomatic solution to the war , but a deal looks more elusive than ever. The root causes of the impasse may be irreconcilable. Why it matters: In the last 18 months, two failed rounds of negotiations have led to two wars. The June MOU collapsed within days and led to renewed escalation. If the current effort to reach a diplomatic breakthrough ends in a deadlock, another outbreak of fighting is likely within weeks. Here's a look at some of the deep-seated dynamics between the two countries — personal, cultural, and political — that have stymied efforts to broker a deal: "Trump has ADD; Iran has OCD" One reason for the failures is that the U.S. and Iran see the timeframe for negotiations very differently. Trump is all about getting a quick deal — he gets impatient and frustrated when things move slowly. The Iranian negotiation style is the complete opposite. They are all about playing for time. "America under Trump is the attention-deficit superpower ... incapable of sustaining a strategy. Iran under the Islamic Republic is the obsessive-compulsive theocracy, fixated on resisting America far more than advancing the welfare of its own people," Karim Sadjadpour, a senior analyst at the Carnegie Endowment, told Axios. "Trump has ADD; Iran has OCD." For example, in April 2025 Trump set a deadline for negotiations at 60 days — an extremely short and unrealistic timetable. The Iranians, on the other hand, saw the negotiations as a longer process and didn't take the deadline seriously enough. They didn't think Trump meant it when he said 60 days. The negotiations in February of this year were even shorter — around three weeks. The chances of getting a deal that quickly were close to zero. A megadeal vs. a narrow truce Trump loves a splashy show of political theater, with him cast as lead actor. He envisions a legacy-making accord that redefines the relationship between the U.S. and Iran and reshapes the Middle East. The Iranians prefer a narrow, transactional deal that's negotiated indirectly — or with the lowest public profile possible. They view any deal as a truce rather than a peace agreement. "Trump and his negotiators pride themselves on being dealmakers. In Iranian political culture, the word for compromiser — 'sazeshkar' — is practically a slur," Sadjadpour said. He added: "Iran's leaders were never willing to meet with Trump directly. Had they been willing to do so, I think the outcome of events could have been very different. Trump wants to resolve the conflict; the Islamic Republic's entire identity is premised on continued confrontation with the U.S." A matter of mistrust The fundamental impediment in the negotiations is mistrust. The Iranians claim Trump cheated them twice when he attacked them in the middle of negotiations. Many inside the Iranian regime think any negotiations with the U.S. are just a ruse to mask preparations for a surprise attack. The U.S. side counters it was Iran that cheated when it violated the June 2026 memorandum of understanding, by attacking ships in the Strait of Hormuz days after signing the deal. U.S. officials say that they can't count on the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps or other radical elements inside the regime to abide by any deal they negotiate with more pragmatic members of the regime. Domestic pressure The negotiations are a fraught domestic political issue for both sides. Iran's negotiating team and others inside the regime who support a deal have come under constant attacks back home. It's pushed them to take a harder line in talks. Trump and his negotiators are getting pressure from the right not to cut a deal — and mocked by the left for potentially accepting one that either restores the pre-war status quo or resembles President Obama's 2015 nuclear deal. That kind of criticism made Trump pull back from more moderate positions he took several times over the last 18 months, including earlier this week. What to watch: White House envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner and Vice President Vance still think diplomacy is worth pursuing. But Trump seems much more skeptical. In an interview with Time magazine published on Thursday, he said what Iran is ready to do "is not good enough" for him. "With Iran, I don't think you could ever have peace," he said, reiterating that he's considering resuming major combat operations after the midterms. Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian on Thursday defended the negotiations with the U.S. "We have never and will not run away from dialogue, although the U.S. targeted our country three times despite having signed the agreement," he said, referring to the June MOU. "The U.S. should get rid of the idea that it would bring us to our knees through terror." But other Iranian officials, especially inside the IRGC, think negotiations are useless and that the only way to end the war is by inflicting more costs on the battlefield. What they're saying: "Iran is adopting a strategy toward the United States defined by escalation and continuous offense," Mohammad Ayatollahi Tabaar, associate professor of international affairs at Texas A&M University's Bush School of Government and Public Service, writes in a new Foreign Affairs article . "[The regime] is clear about what it wants — the removal of all U.S. forces from the region — and it is prepared to remain indefinitely on a wartime footing to get it."

Over the last half millennium, societies around the globe competed to divide up the world’s land. Nearly every square inch of soil outside Antarctica is now owned and tucked within national borders. But the oceans have largely been spared that fate. There were times throughout history when countries tried to gate and regulate the seas, but they were too vast to be controlled for long periods. During the Cold War, as technology made it far easier to imagine partitioning the world’s waterways and seabeds, great powers avoided an unrestrained race to grab the oceans. Most governments agreed to deal with them through a patchwork of treaties and multilateral bodies that sought to guarantee freedom of navigation in international waters and assign coastal seabeds to adjacent littoral states.

item.title: Jack Smith faces new lawsuit over congressional phone records
item.description:
Source: Axios Pre-analysis score: 0.34
Sen. Marsha Blackburn (R-Tenn.) sued former special counsel Jack Smith Wednesday, alleging he unlawfully obtained her cellphone toll records during his investigation of Trump and the 2020 election Why it matters: The lawsuit escalates Republicans' efforts to challenge Smith's investigation more than a year after his probe ended. What they're saying: "Through his Arctic Frost witch hunt that targeted conservatives across America and even the President of the United States, Jack Smith perpetrated one of the worst abuses of government power in our nation's history," Blackburn said. "This lawsuit is solely about holding Mr. Smith accountable and ensuring that our nation's justice system can never again be weaponized against the American people. I thank the New Civil Liberties Alliance for their partnership in filing this complaint and for fighting to uphold our cherished constitutional rights." Driving the news: The suit was filed in the U.S. District Court for the Middle District of Tennessee one day after Smith testified at a Senate Judiciary Committee hearing Tuesday. The suit alleges Smith obtained a nondisclosure order without telling the judge that the underlying subpoena sought the records of a sitting senator. Blackburn's cellphone provider was ordered to keep the subpoena secret. Blackburn is asking the court to award her $1 in nominal damages to emphasize that she isn't seeking money but instead wants to hold Smith accountable for his allegedly unlawful actions. Legal counsel for Smith did not immediately respond to Axios' request for comment. Flashback: The lawsuit comes one day after Sen. Eric Schmitt (R-Mo.), a potential running mate for JD Vance in 2028, accused Smith of perjury at Tuesday's hearing but got his facts wrong and was later corrected by Smith and Sen. Amy Klobuchar (D-Minn.). The mistake went viral and drew extensive criticism on social media. Catch up quick: In October 2025, the GOP-led House Judiciary Committee released highly redacted documents showing that the FBI had investigated approximately 160 Republican figures as part of its probe into Trump's false claims that the 2020 presidential election was stolen. The probe, known as Arctic Frost, sought to identify those who "conspired to corruptly obstruct the United States Congress' certification of the 2020 Presidential election results by submitting allegedly fraudulent elector certificates." By the numbers: The lawsuit claims the Arctic Frost probe subpoenaed records associated with at least 20 Republican members of Congress. The lawsuit claims about 400 Republican individuals and organizations were targeted. The lawsuit says records involving roughly 4,782 Trump donors, including 102 Tennesseans, contained home addresses, bank account numbers and signatures. The bottom line: Blackburn's lawsuit extends the legal and political fight over the Justice Department's investigations into Trump after he left office. Trump and his allies have vowed to continue probing those who investigated or crossed the president, including New York Attorney General Letitia James (D), former FBI chief James Comey and Sen.
